titre: The sprint in three parts, and a page for each story
changements: The sprint page is split in three: the sprint itself (where it stands, the go, closing it), the work in progress (Claude's runs, the next story to launch, the pull requests open on its stories with merge, update and review), and the features and their stories (stage, testing, priority).
Each story of the sprint opens its own page: its steps from ready to production (done, current, to come), its acceptance criteria, its pull requests, Claude's runs and its history from the log.

titre: Give the go from the sprint; the sprint closes once it is out
changements: On a project with an integration branch, the sprint offers the go itself, as Production does: what production will receive, the stories validated or not, the next release to open (minor or major).

A go given from the sprint closes it once the promotion is out: the validated stories are closed, each finished card takes the version just released, and a card not finished stays for the next sprint.

titre: The sprint leads to the go
changements: On a project with an integration branch, the sprint says how its release is made: test the stories on int, give the go in Production (linked), then close the sprint so that each finished card takes its version.
The reference-branch banner no longer shows on the board and the sprint, which do not read a branch.

titre: Testing, followed in the sprint and on the card; ticking a criterion at once
changements: A story on int (or merged, without integration) says where its testing stands, in the sprint and on its card: Validated, by whom and when, or how many of its criteria are checked, with a link to test it.

In To test, ticking a criterion shows at once and is saved in the background, without reloading the page; Validate unlocks as soon as every criterion is ticked. If GitHub refuses, the tick goes back and the page says why.

titre: Clearer pull requests in the sprint; no branch menu where it does nothing
changements: Ask for a review no longer shows an empty list: when there is no one else to ask (the author of a pull request cannot review it, and the reviewers are La Fabrique's tech leads and super admins), the sprint says so.
On a project without a merge workflow, the sprint says where to merge a pull request (on GitHub) and what to declare in Setup (workflows.fusionner).
The reference-branch menu is gone from the board, the cards and the sprint, which do not read a branch.

titre: Merging puts work online; closing the sprint makes the release
changements: Once Close the sprint starts the release, the sprint says it is in progress, with a link to follow it on GitHub, and updates by itself; if it fails, it says why (from the run) and the sprint stays open to close again.
The release no longer stops on a test that expected changes waiting right after a release.

La Fabrique declares its release workflow (workflows.publier): Close the sprint now makes its release instead of saying none is declared. The workflow turns the release-note entries of the stories done into one entry (the version chosen, the date and time, the title, every change, the stories), marks an entry with a story not done yet as partial and names it, keeps the other entries for a later release, checks, then merges a pull request on main, which deploys.
Before the close, a warning lists the merged stories not done and the partial release-note entries, says their changes stay online but are kept for a later release, and lets you postpone or go on.
A release-note entry with at least one done story is released marked partial, with a caveat naming the stories not done; those stories stay open in To test.

On a project without an integration branch, a Product Engineer or super admin who clicks Close the sprint chooses minor or major (numbers proposed after the newest release), sees what the release takes and what stays, each with its reason, edits the proposed title, and starts the project's release workflow (workflows.publier, documented in Setup). A project that has not declared it is refused with a link to Setup.

Once the release workflow succeeds, the sprint closes, each done card takes the new version and its validated stories are closed with a comment; the close, the release started and out, each card versioned and each story closed are in the project log.
Tech leads and testers do not get Close the sprint on such a project.
A sprint no longer closes by itself when its needed stories are in production: a Product Engineer or super admin closes it with Close the sprint.
Stop the sprint is gone.
A card that is not finished stays in the Sprint lane for the next sprint, with its stories already in production folded under it as done.
On a project without an integration branch, merging deploys the change and no longer gives it a version number: its release-notes entry stays next until the release.
The (i) and /api/version show the last release plus what is online since (0.78 + 3 changes); What's new lists these entries under Online, not released yet, above the last release.
Validating a merged story on such a project no longer closes its issue: it stays To test, online and not released.

titre: One status for a card, from the spec to production
changements: A card has one status. Draft, Shaping, To validate and Validated say where its spec stands; once Validated with stories, the status follows them by itself: Stories to prepare, Ready for dev, In sprint, In development, To test, In production, with its count (In development 1/3 developed) and, on hovering, every count (3 stories: 3 ready, 2 developed, 1 validated, 0 in production).

The board's Status lanes have these stages; a card cannot be moved into or out of them by hand, only to To validate (the feature changed) or Dropped. The card's page says since when, and the stages it went through.
A pull request no longer writes a version number in the release notes: its entry says next, and the merge gives the number and the time.

titre: Why a merge was refused
changements: When the merge workflow refuses a pull request (conflicts with main and in which files, checks failing, not open, a draft), it says why: in a comment on the pull request, in the log, and in the sprint next to the pull request, with the run.

titre: Choose the next release with the go
changements: Before giving the go, you choose how the next release is numbered: minor (1.4 → 1.5, by default) or major (1.4 → 2.0).
Once the go is given, La Fabrique opens a pull request in your name on the integration branch that adds the next release with an empty release note; the project merges it.
The project's log keeps who gave the go, the next number chosen, and the pull request.

titre: Product Engineers can give the go to production
changements: Product Engineers can now give the go that pushes the version on integration to production, like the super admin; tech leads and testers cannot (the page hides it and the request is refused). Merging a pull request into the production branch follows the same rule.

titre: A card's progress, from its stories
changements: Besides its status (where the spec stands: Draft to Validated), a card has a progress, worked out from its stories and the sprint, never typed: Stories to prepare (2/3 ready), Ready for dev, In sprint, In development (1/3 developed), To test (2/3 validated), In production. The nice to have count only when all of a card's stories are.

The progress shows on the board's cards, the card's page (since when, and the stages it went through) and the sprint; the board can be laid out by Progress (Lane or Group by), and a card is not moved across it by hand.
Each change of progress is written in the log, dated.

titre: To validate, on the dashboard and in the sprint; the merge workflow in Setup
changements: Without an integration branch, the dashboard shows how many stories are To validate, linked to To test.
In the sprint, a story To validate points to To test, where its criteria are checked.
Setup says whether the project declares its merge workflow (workflows.fusionner), and how to write one.

titre: Stories validated on int are closed once in production
changements: When the project's promotion workflow ends well, La Fabrique closes the stories of that go that were validated on int, with a word on each (in the project's language), and writes it in the log; a story sent anyway, without its validation, stays open and To validate. The sprint then sees them shipped and closes by itself.

titre: Merge from the sprint, release notes numbered at the merge
changements: A project can declare its merge workflow (workflows.fusionner): Merge on a pull request of the sprint starts it; into the production branch it is a go, for the super admin only, into another branch a tech lead can.

La Fabrique's own merge workflow numbers and dates the pull request's release-notes entries at the merge (after main's newest, at the time of the merge), checks again, then squash-merges: two pull requests written at the same time no longer conflict on the next version number.

titre: A merged story waits for its validation
changements: A story whose pull request is merged, but still open, is now To validate (it stayed In development): its work is in, its acceptance criteria still have to be checked.

Without an integration branch (La Fabrique itself), To test lists the stories to validate in production, with their criteria to tick, Validate and Report a defect; validated, a story is done and its issue closed, so the sprint counts it as shipped.

titre: A story's pull request, linked for sure; Update with Claude
changements: A pull request belongs to the story GitHub links it to (a branch created from the issue, a pull request that closes it) or whose number its branch carries; a pull request that only mentions a story in its text is shown as guessed from its text, and one that cites another issue in passing is no longer attached to it.
When a Claude run ends, the log says which pull request it opened, or which one it brought up to date, with the run.

In the sprint, a pull request in conflict with its base branch, or behind it, says so; Update with Claude (tech lead and above) has Claude merge the base branch into it, resolve the conflicts, check again and push to the same pull request.

La Fabrique's Claude workflow, and the example in Setup, create the story's branch linked to its issue, open a pull request that starts with Refs #N (the story stays open until it is validated) and say how each acceptance criterion is checked; they take a pr input to bring a pull request up to date.

titre: The go says what blocks it
changements: The go is shown as blocked, with the reason: the stories on int that are not validated (listed; the super admin can still give the go anyway by saying why), a failing check on the integration branch, or nothing new since the last production version.

titre: What's new in La Fabrique
changements: A What's new page lists La Fabrique's own releases, newest first: date and time, what changed, and the stories each one brought (linked to GitHub when La Fabrique is one of its own projects).
The (i) next to the name leads to it, at the version running.

titre: The sprint follows Claude's work and its pull requests
changements: The sprint updates by itself when Claude starts or ends a run, or when a pull request moves on GitHub; the end of each run is written in the log.
Each story of the sprint shows its pull requests (open, draft, merged) and who was asked to review them; Ask for a review asks a tech lead or super admin, on GitHub, in your name.

titre: Follow Claude's runs from the sprint
changements: The sprint shows Claude's runs: those in progress at the top, and on each story the state of its last run (queued, working, done, failed, cancelled), linked to the run on GitHub; Every Claude run on GitHub, and Refresh. A story whose run is in progress is not launched twice.
La Fabrique's Claude workflow accepts being started by La Fabrique's GitHub App (it stopped at once before), and names each run after its story (Claude #12); the example workflow too.

When GitHub refuses to start a project's workflow (Launch Claude, the go), La Fabrique says why: HTTP 403, the App may not run the repository's workflows (Actions in read and write, accepted on the installation); HTTP 404, the workflow is not on the branch GitHub starts it from.

titre: What version is running
changements: An (i) next to La Fabrique's name: on hover or focus, the version running, when it was released (Paris time) and its commit, with Update, which reloads when a newer version is out and says so otherwise.

titre: Claude's setup explained, and the Definition of Ready one click away
changements: Setup explains the Claude workflow step by step: the workflow file and its examples, the two ways to give Claude its key (a subscription token or an API key), the token that lets its pull request run the CI, and the cap.
The sprint and the backlog link to the project's Definition of Ready, changed from Setup (Story lifecycle) as a pull request on the project; a story made from a card is said to meet the epic check.

titre: Getting the sprint's stories ready, and priorities from the card
changements: A story made from a card no longer needs an epic to be ready: the card groups it, as an epic would.
In the sprint, each story not ready says what it lacks, and it is fixed there: its priority, Mark ready (the project's ready label), or a link to add its criteria on GitHub.
A card has a priority, set on its page or in the sprint: its stories take it, one level lower for those nice to have; the stories made from it later take it too.
When Claude splits a spec into stories, it says which are nice to have; the preview lets you change it before GitHub.

titre: Claude Code from the sprint
changements: The sprint says which story comes next for Claude: the first ready one not launched yet, in the sprint's order. Launch the next story starts it; each ready story of the sprint has its own Launch Claude, and says who launched it and when.
It runs the project's own Claude workflow, at most as many at once as the project allows; when GitHub or the cap refuses, the sprint says why. Tech leads and the super admin only.
La Fabrique declares its own Claude workflow: Claude Code makes a branch from main, does the story, runs the tests and opens a pull request to main, never merged without you.

titre: Next release, a sprint without a version, and the order in the sprint
changements: Next release: a lane of the board with no version, always first after Not set, where the next sprint is prepared. Planning a release by number is gone: a numbered release could ship with other work and carry its cards away undone.

Start the sprint (Sprint tab) takes the cards of Next release into the Sprint lane. The sprint closes by itself once every needed story of its cards is in production: each card takes the version that shipped it, what is not done goes back to Next release. Close the sprint and Stop the sprint do it by hand.

In the sprint and in Next release, move cards up or down (the board's order follows), and a card's stories up or down; mark a story nice to have: done if there is time, it does not count in the stories left.
The backlog grouped by card shows each card's stories in the same order, with nice to have marked.

titre: The sprint
changements: A Sprint tab: the release we work on, its cards, and under each card its stories with their stage; how many are in production; the stories its release notes declare that come from no card.

Start the sprint on a planned release: it becomes in progress (Sprint on the board). One sprint at a time; Stop the sprint plans it again. It ends by itself when the project's release notes date the release.
Without a sprint started, the Sprint tab shows the release in progress on the project's integration branch.

titre: Stories and backlog, grouped by card
changements: Stories: Group by Card shows the stories of each card together, under the card's id, title, status and release; the newest release first; the stories from no card last.
Backlog: Group by Priority or Card; by card, each card's stories not started yet, the ready ones first. Setting a priority keeps the grouping.
A story made from two cards appears under each, saying where else it is (also in C8).

titre: Import cards, and releases spelled like the project's
changements: Import cards (JSON), under the board: a file in the export's format, or pasted. Each card comes in as a new card with its text, tags, release, spec and stories; a card whose title is already on the board is skipped, so importing twice adds nothing.
A planned release is spelled as the project's release notes write their versions: on the épicerie, 1.170 after 1.169 (not v1.170, nor v1.1).

titre: A compact board header; Not set first
changements: The board's header fits on one or two lines: Lane and Group by (were Columns and Then rows), the hide box, Filters, the count, and the buttons.
New lane, New group and Plan a release are buttons in the header, always there (they were at the end of the board, and gone when empty lanes were hidden). Plan a release suggests the next version.
The Not set lane comes first, so the cards not placed yet stay in sight.
The project's older releases, written before release times were, show as shipped (they showed as in progress).

titre: The project's releases on the board
changements: Arranged by release, the board shows the project's own releases, read from its release notes: shipped, and the one in progress. They go from the newest on the left to the oldest on the right, each with its state and its title on hover.
By release, Hide empty lanes becomes Hide closed lanes: it hides only shipped releases with no card; the release in progress and those planned stay visible.
Plan a release ahead from the board: it follows the project's numbering (v1.N, 0.N…) and comes after the last one out; the field suggests the next number.

titre: When the feature changes, its stories are reviewed
changements: A validated card whose feature changes (its text, its spec, an older version brought back) goes back to To validate, with the reason in the journal.

Once a card has stories, Split into stories with Claude becomes Review the stories with Claude: Claude reads the stories already made (their stage and criteria) against the spec, and says which still fit, which to change, and which new stories are missing.
You review it all before GitHub: the comment for each story to change (edited, sent in your name, with a link to the card's spec version) and the new stories; then the card is Validated again.

titre: What comes next on a spec, in one row
changements: On a card's spec, what can come next is in one row: Split into stories with Claude first, Make one story on GitHub next to it, then Ask Claude for a change and Edit the spec by hand. A line says when to choose one story or several.
Every button that calls Claude carries a star, here, in Settings and on the backlog.
One panel at a time unfolds under the row, with its title.

titre: From one card to several stories, reviewed before GitHub
changements: Split into stories with Claude: from a card's spec, Claude proposes stories that can each be built, tested on int and shipped alone, each with its own criteria. It works in the background, like the spec, and nothing goes to GitHub yet.

Review and create the stories: uncheck those you do not want, edit their titles and sections, see exactly what GitHub will receive, then create the checked ones in one go. What GitHub refuses stays proposed; Save my edits and Discard the proposal are there too.
Each story links back to its card at a permanent address (/c/12) and to the version of the spec it came from; a story made from a split says which one it is (story 2 of 3).
The card lists its stories with their stage (backlog, in development, on int, in production) and how many are in production.

titre: A card's status, from its page and by itself
changements: A card's status is changed right on its page, without Edit.

It also follows the card's work: Shaping when Claude is asked, To validate when Claude knows enough or the questions are closed, Validated when its story is made. It only moves forward, never off Dropped nor on an archived card, and the log says why.

titre: Asking Claude starts with a button
changements: On a card, Write the spec with Claude and Ask Claude for a change are buttons first: each unfolds what Claude will do, the field and Ask Claude (or Cancel); once sent, the widget that follows Claude's work takes their place.

titre: Claude works in the background, and shows what it does
changements: Writing, revising or answering Claude's questions no longer waits on the page: the request and your answers are saved at once, Claude works in the background, and you can leave the page or close it without losing anything.

On the card, a widget says what Claude is doing and for how long; unfold it to read its log: what it reads, what it thinks, each section as it writes it, its questions, the cost. It is pushed to the page as it happens. The board marks the cards where Claude is working.
When Anthropic is busy, Claude tries again by itself, up to three times; if it still cannot finish, the card says why, keeps your request, and Try again sends it again.
Claude stops asking when it knows enough to write the stories, and says why; Enough questions closes them when you decide it knows enough. Everything happens in the page, without a window.

titre: Hide the empty lanes of the board
changements: Board: "Hide empty lanes" (next to Columns and Then rows) shows only the columns and rows that hold a card, filters included; kept on the device with the rest of the arrangement.

titre: Writing a card's spec with Claude, as a conversation
changements: Claude frames the need before writing it out: it asks what the card leaves open (who, when, what counts as done, the edge cases), at most five questions, the most decisive first, and leaves a section empty rather than invent it.

Each of Claude's questions has its own answer field under the spec; Send my answers to Claude revises the spec with them. The questions answered are kept with the spec, and Claude does not ask them again.
Write the spec with Claude and Ask Claude for a change open in a window; while Claude writes, the button says so and the request is sent only once.

titre: A defect is about a change of the release note
changements: What a defect is about shows each version's release note in detail: every change can be chosen, in the report form of the project's app (report kit 1.2.0) and in triage, as well as the stories the version declares. The change chosen is quoted in the issue, kept in the log, and shown on the defect's page and in the Defects list.
A change of a version that declares a single story links that story.

titre: Defects are about what the release notes say
changements: What a defect can be about, when reported from a project's app or triaged, now comes from the release notes only: each version with the stories its entry declares. Nothing is guessed any more from branches or dates, so stories left open no longer show up.

A release-notes entry declares its stories in a new stories field (issue numbers). Releases shows them; an entry that does not declare them keeps the stories closed since the previous version as a hint.

titre: A page for each defect
changements: Defects tab: each defect opens on its own page, with the issue as GitHub has it (text, screenshot, comments), the story it is about in a preview (its text and how many criteria are met), and its history in the log.

Triage is done on that page, with the same list as the report form of the project's app: the versions on int, then those released, each with its stories, a search, and the earlier versions on demand. The Defects list and To test lead to the page.

titre: Triage defects, and find them in To test
changements: Defects tab: testers and up triage a defect with the same choice as the report form, a version and one of its stories; La Fabrique says it on GitHub, on the story and on the defect, and removes the to triage label.
To test shows each story with its defects as triage left them, and lists the defects not linked to a story yet, with a link to triage them.
Each triage is in the project's log.

titre: A card's spec with Claude, and the story made from it
changements: On a card, Claude writes its functional spec in the project's own request sections, from the card, the project's CLAUDE.md, its other cards and its open stories; it asks its questions next to the spec. Revise with Claude by answering them or saying what should change, or edit the spec by hand. Every version is kept and can be restored.
Make the story: once the required sections are filled in, the spec becomes an issue on GitHub in your name, with a link back to the card; the card lists its stories.

Claude is used by Product Engineers, tech leads and super admins only, with quotas: calls per person and day, and a monthly budget for all of La Fabrique. Every call is recorded with its tokens and its cost, never its content.

What Claude cost shows on each card and on the board; Settings shows whether Claude is set up, the model, the quotas, and for the super admin the spend by project, person and card, the last calls, and a key check.

titre: Keep a project's report kit up to date
changements: Setup → Connected app says which version of the report kit the project keeps, against the latest, and what the app's relay must follow.
One button proposes the update as a pull request on the integration branch, under your GitHub name: the project reviews it, tries it on int and merges it.
La Fabrique's pull requests carry the project's marker for changes nothing a user sees (version.coulisses), so the project's checks let them through.

titre: Defects tab, and what a defect is about
changements: Each project has a Defects tab: the issues labelled bug, open or closed, with the story and the version each is about, who reported it, its screenshot, and those left to triage.

The report form of the project's app asks what the defect is about: the versions on int first, each with its stories, then the versions released with the stories they brought; a search finds an older one, and I don't know is always possible.
The issue is linked to the story chosen and says which version it is about; the report kit is now 1.1.0.

titre: The report kit
changements: A Report a defect button any project can add to its own app: the person picks the part of the page that is wrong (Wider, This one, The whole page), writes two lines, and can attach a screenshot of that part; the issue is opened in their name.

Three files to copy into the app, with no dependency and nothing loaded from elsewhere, and a small relay on the app's server, described step by step in the guide; Setup → Connected app points to them.
Reports made without network are kept on the device and sent when it is back; the page's recent errors go with each report.

titre: Perspectives and the board of cards
changements: Perspectives: choose in the header what you see. Product shows a project's board, stories, backlog, what to test, roadmap, releases and requests; Administration shows production, delivery, activity, the log and setup; All keeps every tab. A perspective hides tabs, it never removes a right; a Product Engineer starts in Product.

Each project has a Board: cards written in La Fabrique, before they become stories (if ever). A card is a title and a few lines of Markdown, with a type (feature, idea, question), a status (draft, shaping, to validate, validated, dropped) and the project's own epic, domain, segment and release.

Arrange the board by one dimension, then by another to cross them (domains in columns, segments in rows), and filter it; the arrangement stays on this device. Drag a card by its handle (or Space and the arrow keys): it takes the values of the place it is dropped in. A new column creates a new value.

In a card's text, {segment: pro} sets a tag, #12 links an issue, @login names a person and [[Basket]] marks a term. Every version of a card is kept, every decision is in the project's log, and every card can be exported as JSON.

titre: The project's app in Setup
changements: A project's app is registered from the project's Setup tab: its name and return addresses come from application in .fabrique.json, and the identifiers are shown once with the commands to run in the project.
Setup says whether the app has been used, warns when its return addresses drift from .fabrique.json and fixes them in one click, and renews the secret without disconnecting anyone.
Settings → Connected apps keeps what is personal: the apps you connected, to disconnect them.

titre: Report a defect from the project's app
changements: A project's app reports a defect from the page where it shows up: La Fabrique opens the issue with the page, version, component and screenshot, labels it bug, links it to the story on int when there is one, and signs it with the person's login.
Anyone whose GitHub account sees the project can report, a role or not; reports from an account without a role are labelled to triage. At most 20 a day per account.
Reports are accepted only from an environment declared with signalement in .fabrique.json and that says it is that environment; Setup warns when an environment answers another one than its type.
Rights now follow one ladder: each role can do what the ones below it do (a tech lead can validate on int).

titre: Connected apps
changements: A project's own app can connect to La Fabrique in the name of the person using it, after a consent page (“‹app› will be able to report defects in your name on ‹project›”); it never gets a GitHub token.
Settings → Connected apps lists the apps you connected, with a button to disconnect each; the super admin registers a project's app there and gets its identifiers once.
An account without a role can sign in to connect an app, for a project whose repository it can see on GitHub; the rest of La Fabrique still turns it away.

titre: The project's workflows in Setup
changements: Setup says whether the project has a promotion workflow (for the go) and a Claude workflow (for Launch Claude), what they need, and shows the épicerie's as examples.

titre: Launch Claude
changements: Tech leads and super admins launch Claude on a ready story from the Backlog: La Fabrique starts the project's own Claude workflow with the issue number, labels the story ready for Claude and says so on the issue.
A cap of Claude runs at once per project (2 unless the project says otherwise); each launch is in the log.

titre: Give the go
changements: When production is ready, the super admin gives the go from the Production tab: it shows the stories production will get and who validated each, then starts the project's own promotion workflow.
Stories not validated on int need a reason to go anyway; the go, its reason and the promotion run are kept and shown to everyone.

titre: Log
changements: A Log tab: every decision taken in La Fabrique on a project, newest first, in words and with links to GitHub: requests written, criteria checked, stories validated, defects reported, priorities set, setup changes proposed.
Filter by kind of decision and by person; nothing in it can be changed or deleted.

titre: A logo, a project menu
changements: La Fabrique has a logo: a sawtooth-roofed workshop, also in the browser tab.
With several projects, the project's name in the header opens a menu to switch to another one, on the same tab.
Links to GitHub and to the projects' environments open in a new tab.

titre: Validate on int
changements: On To test, testers, Product Engineers and super admins tick each acceptance criterion: it is ticked in the GitHub issue too.
Validate a story once every criterion is checked: the issue gets a comment with the int version, the to-validate label goes, and La Fabrique keeps who validated and when.
Report a defect from a story: it becomes a GitHub issue linked to the story, listed under it until fixed.
What La Fabrique writes in a project follows its language (langue in .fabrique.json).

titre: Change the story lifecycle from Setup
changements: Setup has a Story lifecycle section: the Definition of Ready checks and the priority labels, read from the project's .fabrique.json.

Super admins and tech leads propose a change from there: La Fabrique opens a pull request on the project, under their GitHub name, that changes only the lifecycle; the project reviews and merges it as usual.

titre: Dashboard
changements: The home page is now a dashboard: one card per project with what needs attention now (to test on int, production ready or not, in development and stalled work, ready to start, top priority in the backlog, CI on production, versions, last release), each figure leading to its tab.
What your role looks at comes first: testers see what to test, tech leads the CI and the work in progress, super admins production.

titre: Backlog and priorities
changements: A Backlog tab: the stories not started yet, by priority, the ready ones first, each with its epic and what its Definition of Ready lacks.
Super admins, tech leads and Product Engineers set a story's priority from the backlog: La Fabrique puts the priority label on GitHub and writes who changed it in its log.
The project tabs keep to one line.

titre: In development
changements: An In development tab: every story being worked on, with its branches, its pull request (draft or not), the CI result of its latest run and its last commit; work without a commit for 3 days is marked stalled.
Working branches that refer to no story are listed apart, with how to link them.

titre: To test
changements: A To test tab answers "what is new on int?": the stories waiting on int, by epic, each with its acceptance criteria as a checklist, the release-notes changes production does not have yet, and a button to open int.
Without an integration branch, it says what the latest production version brought.
On a phone, the tabs scroll sideways on one line.

titre: Where each story stands
changements: Each story has a stage on the Stories board: Backlog, Ready, In development, On int or In production, computed from GitHub, with a stage filter.
A story in the backlog says what its Definition of Ready lacks; each project declares its own Definition of Ready and priority labels in its .fabrique.json (Setup explains how).

titre: Delivery at once
changements: Delivery shows at once, then fills in as GitHub answers, instead of a long wait on the first view; the workflows are read side by side.
The loading light has a hot orange core.

titre: Loading light on more browsers
changements: The red loading light now shows on older browsers too.
Pages keep following one another in place even when the host adds a script of its own to them.
Settings says whether pages follow in place on this device, and which browser it is.

titre: The red light keeps moving, Safari included
changements: La Fabrique now reads the next page itself while the current one stays on screen, so the red loading light keeps sweeping until the page is there, in Safari too.
Back and forward work as before; a page that needs its own script is still loaded by the browser.

titre: Settings
changements: A Settings page: the version online, and whether this device runs the latest stylesheet and script.
Reload everything: the browser forgets what it kept of La Fabrique, and the page comes back from the server; your session stays.
Try a slow page, to see the loading bar at work.

titre: Always the latest look
changements: After each update, pages use the new styles and scripts at once, without waiting for the browser's copy to expire.

titre: A red scanner while pages load
changements: The loading bar is now a red light sweeping back and forth, and it keeps moving while the next page is on its way.

titre: Setup
changements: A Setup tab on each project: what La Fabrique needs to follow it well, read from its files and GitHub, each item done, missing or optional, with how to do it and an example.
An integration branch is optional; the Setup tab explains how to add one.
La Fabrique serves its own .fabrique.json and release-notes format, which the how-to links open.

titre: What production will get
changements: The Production tab opens on what production will get: the stories the pending work refers to, by epic, and every release-notes entry production does not have yet, with a count of stories, versions and changes.

titre: Reference branch in the header
changements: Choose a project's reference branch from a menu in the header, with a search over all its branches; like a checkout, it stays chosen on every tab until you go back to production.
Production compares the chosen branch with production; Activity, Delivery, Releases, Roadmap and the documentation read that branch.
The project, its branch and who you are now share one compact line under the bar.
A thin bar runs at the top of the page while the next one loads.

titre: La Fabrique follows itself
changements: La Fabrique extraordinaire can be added as a project of its own: its documentation, stories, delivery, activity and releases show like any other project's.
The version endpoint gives the version number as well as the deployed commit.

titre: Roadmap and releases
changements: A Roadmap tab: a month calendar of versions released, stories closed and epics done, and each epic's progress day by day.
A Releases tab: every version's notes by day, with the stories closed since the previous version.

titre: Delivery
changements: A Delivery tab: each workflow's runs over 30 days, share passed, median duration, current streak and last failure.

titre: Read a project on another branch
changements: A branch selector on a project's page: read its documentation and its .fabrique.json on integration or a working branch, production staying the reference.

titre: Activity
changements: An Activity tab: commits and lines changed per day over 30 or 90 days, and commits per author.

titre: Requests
changements: Product Engineers, tech leads and super admins write a request from the project's own form; it becomes an issue under their name.
Drafts stay on the device until the request is sent; My requests shows where each one stands.

titre: What awaits production
changements: A Production tab: the work on integration missing from production, grouped by merged branch, with versions, workflows and a clear ready or not ready.

titre: Stories
changements: A Stories tab: issues grouped by epic, with their state, labels, pull requests and branches, and filters.

titre: Documentation online
changements: A project's documentation reads in La Fabrique, from its production branch, with links between pages kept inside.

titre: La Fabrique extraordinaire
changements: The app is now called La Fabrique extraordinaire.

titre: Projects
changements: Super admins add a project from the repositories where the GitHub App is installed; its .fabrique.json is checked, with readable errors.

titre: Sign in with GitHub
changements: Sign in with GitHub; only people given a role get in, and super admins manage roles on the People page.

titre: First version
changements: La Fabrique is online, with its home page.
